title: Chapter 29.  Media, Communications & Press Freedom in J&K

blocks.content: The state of media freedom and communications access in J&K has been an actively and internationally discussed subject, particularly regarding internet restrictions imposed around the 2019 reorganisation and subsequent security situations — a topic that intersects directly with the current-affairs material of Chapter 29.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Freedom of speech and expression, including press freedom, is derived from Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).
The Jammu & Kashmir Media Policy 2020 was promulgated to streamline government advertisements, enhance media outreach, and curb fake news in the Union Territory.
In the landmark Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) ruling, the Supreme Court held that freedom of speech and trade over the internet is constitutionally protected.
The Directorate of Information and Public Relations (DIPR) serves as the primary government nodal agency for press communications and accreditation in J&K.

blocks.content: Freedom of speech and expression through the medium of the internet is an integral part of Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

In the immediate aftermath of the August 2019 abrogation of Article 370, the Government of India imposed an extensive security lockdown in J&K that included a prolonged suspension of mobile and internet services, alongside restrictions on landline connectivity in parts of the Kashmir Valley — widely reported at the time as one of the longest internet shutdowns imposed by any democracy, drawing significant domestic and international criticism on communications-freedom and economic-disruption grounds, alongside government justification citing the need to prevent misinformation-driven unrest during the transition.

Internet services were restored in phases over the following months and into 2020, with 4G mobile internet access — restricted to 2G speeds for an extended period even after broader restoration — fully returned only in February 2021, following sustained legal and civil-society advocacy, including a significant Supreme Court judgment (Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, January 2020) that held internet access to be integral to the exercise of fundamental rights under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), while stopping short of ordering an immediate, unconditional restoration and instead directing periodic administrative review of restrictions.

Subsequent to this extended 2019-21 period, more localised, shorter-duration internet suspensions have periodically been imposed in specific circumstances (such as around particular security incidents or public examinations, to prevent malpractice), a pattern also seen in various other Indian states, rather than being unique to J&K, though J&K's overall historical frequency and duration of such restrictions has been notably higher than most other parts of India.

★ EXAM POINT: Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (Supreme Court, January 2020) is the key legal-precedent case on this topic — it held that internet access is integral to fundamental rights but did NOT order an immediate blanket restoration, instead requiring periodic administrative review — a nuanced verdict frequently mis-simplified in either direction by candidates.

items: J&K has a well-established local media landscape, including long-running English and Urdu-language newspapers (such as Greater Kashmir and Kashmir Times, among others) alongside numerous local-language and digital news outlets, operating within India's broader constitutional free-press framework.

Press-freedom advocacy organisations (both Indian and international) have periodically raised concerns regarding restrictions on journalists' movement, allegations of intimidation, and, at various points, the application of security laws to journalists and media organisations in J&K — concerns that the government has generally characterised as necessary security measures applied narrowly and lawfully rather than as a broader press-freedom restriction; this remains a genuinely contested area of assessment between different observers.

The 2020 Jammu and Kashmir Media Policy, introduced by the UT administration, established a framework for government empanelment/accreditation of media outlets tied to compliance with specified content guidelines — a policy that drew both government defence (as a standard, legitimate empanelment mechanism) and civil-society criticism (as potentially enabling denial of government advertising/access to critical outlets) from different quarters.
Supreme Court ruling in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India established that indefinite internet suspensions are illegal and subject to judicial review.
The Media Policy 2020 empowers DIPR to monitor content for fake news and security concerns before issuing official advertisements.
Article 19(2) allows the State to impose reasonable restrictions on press freedom on grounds of sovereignty, integrity, and public order.
Extensive internet/communications shutdown followed the August 2019 abrogation; widely reported as one of the longest such shutdowns imposed by any democracy at the time.
Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (SC, Jan 2020): internet access held integral to fundamental rights, but no immediate blanket restoration ordered — periodic administrative review required instead.
Full 4G mobile internet restored only in February 2021, following a phased 2019-21 restoration process.
2020 J&K Media Policy established a government media-empanelment framework, drawing both defence and criticism from different quarters.
